definition: real and able to be touched or clearly seen

examples.text: The fossil is tangible evidence that the species once lived this far north.
The treaty brought tangible benefits: lower tariffs and open ports.
After months of practice, a medal felt like tangible proof that I had improved.

confused.note: Tangible means real and touchable; tangential means only slightly related.

questions.passage: Supporters of the reading program had long claimed that it worked. This year they could finally point to ______ results: test scores in the participating schools rose by an average of twelve points.
questions.explanation: Measured gains in scores are real, concrete results.

distractors.why: Cryptic means puzzling, which measured scores are not.
Covert means secret, which published results are not.
Punitive means intended to punish, which does not fit.

definition: a feeling of pleasure mixed with sadness when thinking about the past

examples.text: The novel is soaked in nostalgia for a village that no longer exists.
Nostalgia for the old empire shaped the politics of the new republic.
The smell of chalk fills me with nostalgia for elementary school.

confused.note: Nostalgia is a fond longing for the past; neuralgia is nerve pain.

questions.passage: The exhibition of toys from the 1980s drew crowds of adults in their forties. Many admitted that they had come out of ______, hoping to see the robots and board games they remembered from childhood.
questions.explanation: Wanting to see childhood toys again is fond longing for the past.

distractors.why: Remorse is guilt over wrongdoing, which is not why they came.
Adversity is hardship, which does not fit.
Dissent is disagreement, which does not fit.

definition: strong disagreement with an official or widely held opinion

examples.text: The regime tolerated no dissent, and its critics fled abroad.
There was little dissent among the reviewers: the study was sound.
My suggestion of a six a.m. practice met with loud dissent.

confused.note: Dissent is disagreement; descent is a downward movement or one's ancestry.

questions.passage: The council's votes are usually unanimous. On the question of the new stadium, however, there was considerable ______: five of the eleven members spoke against the plan and refused to sign the final report.
questions.explanation: Members speaking against the plan and refusing to sign is disagreement.

distractors.why: Nostalgia is longing for the past, which does not fit.
Renown is fame, which does not fit.
Clemency is mercy, which does not fit.

definition: done in a secret or hidden way

examples.text: The agency ran covert operations in three neighboring countries.
Covert cameras recorded the nocturnal animals without disturbing them.
I gave my friend a covert nod when the teacher asked who knew the answer.

confused.note: Covert means hidden; overt means open. They are opposites.

questions.passage: Officially the two countries had broken off all contact. In practice their diplomats continued to hold ______ talks, meeting in the back room of a restaurant in a third country under false names.
questions.explanation: Talks held under false names in a back room are secret.

distractors.why: Audible means able to be heard, which is not the contrast with "officially."
Sublime means awe-inspiring, which does not fit.
Stringent means strict, which does not describe secret meetings.

definition: to behave in the way that is expected or accepted; to follow a rule or standard

examples.text: Guild members who refused to conform to the dress code were fined.
The new bridge must conform to earthquake safety standards.
I refused to conform and wore sneakers to the formal dance.

confused.note: To conform is to follow a standard; to confirm is to verify.

questions.passage: The school expected its students to ______. Those who dressed differently, asked too many questions, or chose unusual subjects were quietly encouraged to behave more like their classmates.
questions.explanation: Being pressed to behave like everyone else is being made to follow expectations.

distractors.why: Dissent means to disagree openly, which the school discouraged.
Procure means to obtain, which does not fit.
Dispel means to drive away, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin forma, "shape": to shape together

definition: to love, protect, and care for something or someone; to keep a hope or memory in mind

examples.text: She cherishes the one letter her father wrote from the front.
The colonists cherished the right to elect their own assembly.
I cherish the hour before anyone else in the house wakes up.

confused.note: To cherish is to treasure; to perish is to die.

questions.passage: The retired teacher kept every card her students had ever given her. She ______ them, she said, more than any award, and on difficult days she would take down the box and read a few.
questions.explanation: Keeping and rereading the cards shows she treasured them.

distractors.why: Impeded means obstructed, which does not fit.
Averted means turned away or prevented, which does not fit.
Procured means obtained, which does not capture her affection for them.

definition: a strong feeling of guilt and regret about something you have done

examples.text: Tormented by remorse, the thief returns the ring at dawn.
The general expressed no remorse for the burning of the town.
I felt remorse the moment I snapped at my little sister.

confused.note: Remorse is guilt; remote means far away.

questions.passage: The driver who had caused the accident showed genuine ______. He visited the injured cyclist in the hospital every week, paid her medical bills without being asked, and wrote to her family to apologize.
questions.explanation: Visiting, paying, and apologizing show guilt and regret.

distractors.why: Renown is fame, which does not fit.
A veneer is a thin surface layer or false front, which would mean his feeling was not genuine.
Nostalgia is longing for the past, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin mordere, "to bite": biting back

definition: so beautiful or impressive that it inspires awe

examples.text: The poet struggles to describe the sublime view from the summit.
Travelers of the 1800s crossed the Alps in search of sublime scenery.
My grandmother's apple pie is, in my opinion, sublime.

confused.note: Sublime means awe-inspiring; subliminal means below the level of conscious awareness.

questions.passage: Hikers who reach the ridge at sunrise are rewarded with a ______ sight. Below them a sea of cloud fills the valley, and beyond it a line of snow peaks turns from gray to gold.
questions.explanation: A view of glowing peaks above the clouds inspires awe.

distractors.why: Somber means dark and gloomy, the opposite of a glorious sunrise.
Devious means sneaky, which does not describe a view.
Opaque means not see-through, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin limen, "threshold": up to the lintel

definition: loud enough to be heard

examples.text: The bat's calls are too high-pitched to be audible to humans.
Her sigh was barely audible above the ticking of the clock.
The teacher's whisper was audible in the back row, which was unfortunate for her.

confused.note: Audible means able to be heard; edible means safe to eat.

questions.passage: The old recording is badly damaged, and for long stretches only hissing can be heard. In a few passages, however, the singer's voice is clearly ______, and those moments explain why she was so famous.
questions.explanation: Passages where the voice can be heard are loud enough to hear.

distractors.why: Tangible means touchable, which does not describe a voice on a recording.
Cryptic means puzzling, which is not the contrast with hissing.
Lofty means high or noble, which does not fit.

definition: something that comes before another thing and leads to or develops into it

examples.text: The small feathered dinosaur was a precursor of modern birds.
The telegraph was a precursor of the telephone.
Flashcards on paper were the precursor of the app I use now.

confused.note: A precursor comes before; a successor comes after.

questions.passage: The abacus is often described as a ______ of the modern computer. Though it has no electronics, it embodied the same idea: representing numbers by the positions of objects that can be moved according to fixed rules.
questions.explanation: An earlier device embodying the same idea came before and led toward the computer.

distractors.why: A veneer is a thin surface layer, which does not fit.
An insurgent is a rebel, which does not fit.
Adversity is hardship, which does not fit.

definition: very strict and requiring exact obedience

examples.text: The lab follows stringent rules for handling radioactive material.
Stringent rationing kept the besieged city alive through the winter.
The pool has stringent rules: no running, no diving, no glass.

confused.note: Stringent means strict; strident means harsh and loud.

questions.passage: The airline's safety standards are more ______ than the law requires. Its mechanics inspect each engine twice as often as regulations demand, and any pilot who has slept fewer than eight hours is removed from the schedule.
questions.explanation: Inspecting twice as often as required shows very strict standards.

distractors.why: Lax means loose and careless, the opposite of these standards.
Covert means secret, which is not what the examples show.
Sublime means awe-inspiring, which does not describe safety rules.

definition: intended as punishment

examples.text: The victors imposed punitive taxes on the defeated kingdom.
The study compared punitive and rewarding methods of training dogs.
Taking away my phone for a month felt more punitive than necessary.

confused.note: Punitive means punishing; putative means generally supposed.

questions.passage: The fine was not meant simply to recover the cost of the damage. It was ______, set at ten times that amount so that other companies would think twice before dumping waste in the river.
questions.explanation: A fine far above the cost of damage is meant to punish.

distractors.why: Tacit means unspoken, which does not describe a fine.
Audible means able to be heard, which does not fit.
Lofty means high or noble; the sentence explains the fine's purpose, which is punishment.

definition: a difficult or unlucky situation; hardship

examples.text: The settlers showed remarkable courage in the face of adversity.
Adversity brings out a kindness in the hero that comfort never did.
A week without Wi-Fi was the greatest adversity my little brother had ever faced.

confused.note: Adversity is hardship; an adversary is an opponent.

questions.passage: The biography is less a record of triumphs than a study of how its subject responded to ______. Orphaned at ten, bankrupt at thirty, and exiled at fifty, she rebuilt her life each time.
questions.explanation: Being orphaned, bankrupt, and exiled are hardships.

distractors.why: An adversary is an opponent; it resembles the right word but means something else.
Renown is fame, which is not what these events are.
Clemency is mercy, which does not fit.

definition: not letting light through; or difficult to understand

examples.text: Frosted glass is translucent, but a brick wall is opaque.
The poem's opaque final stanza has puzzled readers for a century.
The instructions for the tax form were opaque, so I called my aunt.

confused.note: Opaque means not see-through or hard to understand; opulent means luxurious.

questions.passage: Customers complained that the phone company's pricing was ______. The total on each bill seemed to bear no relation to the advertised rate, and no one at the help desk could explain how it had been calculated.
questions.explanation: Pricing that no one can explain is hard to understand.

distractors.why: Tangible means real and touchable, which is not the complaint.
Stringent means strict, which is not what customers objected to.
Somber means gloomy, which does not fit.

definition: very high; or showing noble ideals; sometimes, proud and superior

examples.text: The charter opened with lofty words about the rights of all people.
The eagle looks down from its lofty perch.
My lofty goal of running every morning lasted until Wednesday.

confused.note: Lofty means high or noble; it has nothing to do with being left-handed.

questions.passage: The organization was founded with ______ aims: to end hunger, to educate every child, and to bring peace to warring nations. Its actual achievements, a few wells and one small school, were more modest.
questions.explanation: Ending hunger and bringing peace are high, noble aims.

distractors.why: Devious means sneaky, which these aims are not.
Covert means secret, which these publicly stated aims were not.
Punitive means punishing, which does not fit.

definition: mysterious and difficult to understand

examples.text: The dying man's cryptic last words, "under the clock," send the heirs searching.
Scholars still argue over the cryptic symbols carved on the stone.
She left a cryptic note on the fridge: "It's handled. Don't ask."

confused.note: Cryptic means puzzling; a critic is a person who judges.

questions.passage: The treasure map was accompanied by a single ______ instruction: "Begin where the old king sleeps and walk toward what he never saw." It took the searchers a year to work out what the sentence meant.
questions.explanation: An instruction that took a year to decode is puzzling.

distractors.why: Audible means able to be heard, which does not describe a written clue.
Tangible means touchable or concrete; the instruction's difficulty is the point.
Stringent means strict, which does not fit.

definition: a person who fights against the government or established authority

examples.text: The insurgents held the mountain passes for two winters.
The heroine hides a wounded insurgent in her father's barn.
The student council's insurgents demanded an end to the dress code.

confused.note: An insurgent is a rebel; resurgent means rising again.

questions.passage: The government claimed to control the whole province. In fact, ______ held most of the countryside, collecting their own taxes and running their own courts in villages the army dared not enter.
questions.explanation: Fighters who run their own taxes and courts against the government are rebels.

distractors.why: Arbiters are people who settle disputes, not rebels.
Precursors are forerunners, which does not fit.
Adversities are hardships, not people.

partsNote: from Latin surgere, "to rise": rising against

definition: to get something, especially with effort or care

examples.text: The quartermaster procured boots for the army from three countries.
The lab struggled to procure enough of the rare isotope.
I somehow procured tickets to a concert that sold out in two minutes.

confused.note: To procure is to obtain; a procedure is a way of doing something.

questions.passage: During the shortage, the hospital's director spent most of her days trying to ______ supplies. She telephoned factories directly, traded with other hospitals, and once drove four hundred miles to collect a single crate of bandages.
questions.explanation: Calling, trading, and driving to collect supplies is obtaining them with effort.

distractors.why: Avert means to prevent or turn away, which does not fit supplies.
Dispel means to drive away, the opposite of obtaining.
Impede means to obstruct, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin curare, "to take care of"

definition: to prevent something bad from happening; or to turn away one's eyes

examples.text: A last-minute treaty averted war between the two kingdoms.
Early warning systems can avert thousands of deaths in a tsunami.
I averted disaster by catching the cake before it slid off the plate.

confused.note: To avert is to prevent or turn away; to advert is to refer to something.

questions.passage: The pilot's quick thinking ______ a catastrophe. Noticing that both engines were losing power, she glided the aircraft onto a stretch of empty highway, and all ninety passengers walked away unhurt.
questions.explanation: Landing safely prevented a disaster.

distractors.why: Procured means obtained, which would mean she brought the catastrophe about.
Cherished means treasured, which does not fit.
Impeded means slowed or obstructed; she prevented the catastrophe entirely.

definition: to delay or block the progress of something

examples.text: Scar tissue can impede the flow of blood through the artery.
Muddy roads impeded the army's retreat.
A broken escalator impeded the morning rush at the station.

confused.note: To impede is to obstruct; to impend is to be about to happen.

questions.passage: Rescue teams reached the village two days later than planned. Their progress had been ______ by landslides, which blocked the only road in six places and had to be cleared by hand.
questions.explanation: Landslides blocking the road slowed their progress.

distractors.why: Averted means prevented entirely, but the teams did arrive.
Dispelled means driven away, a word for doubts and fears, not progress.
Procured means obtained, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin pes, "foot": to shackle the feet

definition: a thin decorative surface; or a pleasant appearance that hides the truth

examples.text: Beneath its veneer of legality, the trial was an act of revenge.
The host's veneer of charm cracks when the wine is spilled.
The desk is cheap pine under a veneer of oak.

confused.note: A veneer is a thin surface or false front; to venerate is to revere.

questions.passage: The company presented itself as a friendly family business. Behind that ______, former employees said, was a workplace where staff were watched by cameras and fined for speaking to one another.
questions.explanation: A friendly image hiding harsh reality is a false surface.

distractors.why: A precursor is a forerunner, which does not fit.
Remorse is guilt, which does not fit.
Dissent is disagreement, which does not fit.

definition: the state of being famous and respected

examples.text: The city won renown for the skill of its glassmakers.
A knight of great renown arrives at the castle gate.
Our town's only renown comes from a very large statue of a potato.

confused.note: Renown is fame; to renounce is to give up.

questions.passage: The surgeon achieved international ______ for a technique she developed in a small rural hospital. Doctors from thirty countries traveled there to watch her operate.
questions.explanation: Doctors traveling from thirty countries show she became famous and respected.

distractors.why: Adversity is hardship, which does not fit.
Clemency is mercy, which does not fit.
Nostalgia is longing for the past, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin nomen, "name": named again and again

definition: to make a doubt, fear, or false belief go away

examples.text: The experiment dispelled the notion that heavier objects fall faster.
The queen appeared on the balcony to dispel rumors of her death.
One taste dispelled my doubts about pineapple on pizza.

confused.note: To dispel is to drive away a belief or feeling; to dispense is to hand out.

questions.passage: Parents worried that the new vaccine had been rushed. To ______ their fears, the health agency published every page of the trial data and held public meetings at which its scientists answered questions for hours.
questions.explanation: Publishing data and answering questions is meant to drive fears away.

distractors.why: Impede means to slow or obstruct, which is not the agency's aim toward fears.
Procure means to obtain, the opposite of removing fears.
Conform means to follow a standard, which does not fit.

definition: dark and gloomy; serious and sad

examples.text: The novel opens on a somber November afternoon.
A somber crowd lined the streets for the funeral procession.
The mood in the locker room was somber after the loss.

confused.note: Somber means gloomy; sober means not drunk, or serious.

questions.passage: The mood at the factory was ______ on its final day. Workers who had spent thirty years together emptied their lockers in near silence, and several stood for a long time at the gate before leaving.
questions.explanation: Silence and lingering at the gate show a sad, serious mood.

distractors.why: Sublime means awe-inspiring, which does not describe a sad farewell.
Elated means overjoyed, the opposite of this mood.
Devious means sneaky, which does not fit.

definition: using dishonest or indirect methods to get what you want

examples.text: The devious steward alters the will while the family is at dinner.
By devious means, the minister had his rivals sent abroad.
My devious sister hid the last cookie inside an empty vegetable bag.

confused.note: Devious means sneaky; deviant means departing from normal standards.

questions.passage: The company's method of raising prices was ______. It left the price on the box unchanged but quietly reduced the amount of cereal inside, hoping that shoppers would not notice.
questions.explanation: Hiding a price increase so shoppers will not notice is dishonest and indirect.

distractors.why: Lofty means noble, the opposite of a sneaky trick.
Audible means able to be heard, which does not fit.
Stringent means strict, which does not describe a trick.

partsNote: from Latin via, "road": off the road

definition: a person with the power to settle a dispute or decide what is acceptable

examples.text: The pope was asked to act as arbiter between the two crowns.
The duchess is the unquestioned arbiter of taste in the town.
Mom is the final arbiter of who gets the front seat.

confused.note: An arbiter is a judge; arbitrary means based on whim.

questions.passage: For three decades the magazine's food critic was the city's ______ of fine dining. A single favorable sentence from her could fill a restaurant for a year, and an unfavorable one could close it.
questions.explanation: Someone whose word decides a restaurant's fate judges what is acceptable.

distractors.why: An insurgent is a rebel, which does not fit.
A precursor is a forerunner, not a judge.
A euphemism is a mild expression, not a person.

definition: wanting to hurt someone who has hurt you; eager for revenge

examples.text: The vindictive countess never forgets the smallest insult.
The victors' vindictive terms left the defeated nation bitter for a generation.
Keying someone's car over a parking space is petty and vindictive.

confused.note: Vindictive means vengeful; vindicate means to clear of blame.

questions.passage: The former manager was not content simply to leave the company. In a ______ final act, he deleted years of customer records and sent an insulting letter about his successor to every client.
questions.explanation: Destroying records and insulting his successor is seeking revenge.

distractors.why: Conciliatory means peacemaking, the opposite of his actions.
Tacit means unspoken, which does not describe such open acts.
Nondescript means lacking distinctive features, which this act was not.

definition: mercy shown by someone with the power to punish

examples.text: The queen granted clemency to the rebels who laid down their arms.
The prisoner's mother walks to the capital to beg for clemency.
I appealed to my teacher's clemency for one more day on the essay.

confused.note: Clemency is mercy; inclement describes harsh weather.

questions.passage: The law allowed for a sentence of twenty years. The judge, noting the defendant's youth and evident regret, showed ______ and ordered two years of community service.
questions.explanation: Giving far less than the allowed sentence is mercy.

distractors.why: Duplicity is deceit, which is not what the judge showed.
Remorse is guilt, which the defendant felt; the judge showed mercy.
Adversity is hardship, which does not fit.

definition: extremely happy and excited

examples.text: Elated by the news, the heroine runs the whole way home.
The elated crew cheered as land came into view after ninety days.
I was elated when my name appeared on the cast list.

confused.note: Elated means overjoyed; it is unrelated to "related."

questions.passage: After four years of rejection letters, the novelist was ______ to learn that a publisher wanted her book. She read the email six times, telephoned everyone she knew, and could not sleep that night.
questions.explanation: Rereading the email and being unable to sleep show great happiness.

distractors.why: Somber means gloomy, the opposite of her reaction.
Impervious means unaffected, but she was thrilled.
Sanctimonious means smugly moral, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin latus, "carried": carried out of oneself

definition: impressive in size or plan, but in a way that seems too ambitious or showy

examples.text: The dictator's grandiose plan for a new capital was never built.
The inventor's grandiose talk of changing the world bores his neighbors.
My grandiose plan to repaint my room stalled after one wall.

confused.note: Grand is neutral praise for something large and fine; grandiose suggests it is overdone.

questions.passage: The mayor announced a ______ scheme to build the tallest tower on the continent. Critics pointed out that the city could not yet afford to repair its bridges or keep its libraries open on weekends.
questions.explanation: A hugely ambitious plan the city cannot afford is overambitious and showy.

distractors.why: Nondescript means plain and unremarkable, the opposite of the tallest tower.
Tacit means unspoken, but the scheme was announced.
Reprehensible means deserving strong condemnation, too harsh for an impractical building plan.

definition: deserving strong criticism; morally wrong

examples.text: Even the general's allies called the massacre reprehensible.
The narrator finds his own cowardice reprehensible.
Cheating a friend out of five dollars is small but still reprehensible.

confused.note: Reprehensible means deserving blame; comprehensible means understandable.

questions.passage: The inquiry found the company's conduct ______. It had known for years that the product was dangerous and had hidden the evidence so that sales would not suffer.
questions.explanation: Hiding known dangers for profit is morally wrong.

distractors.why: Commendable means deserving praise, the opposite of this conduct.
Nondescript means unremarkable, which does not describe serious wrongdoing.
Voracious means extremely hungry or eager, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin prehendere, "to seize": deserving to be held back

definition: understood or agreed without being said

examples.text: There was a tacit agreement between the two armies not to fight on feast days.
Her silence is taken as tacit consent.
My roommate and I have a tacit rule that whoever cooks does not wash up.

confused.note: Tacit describes something understood without words; taciturn describes a person who says little.

questions.passage: No contract was ever signed, and the subject was never discussed. Still, the two rival shops had a ______ understanding that neither would open on Sundays, and for forty years neither did.
questions.explanation: An understanding that was never discussed is unspoken.

distractors.why: Explicit means stated outright, but nothing was said or signed.
Vindictive means vengeful, which does not fit.
Grandiose means overambitious, which does not fit.

definition: a mild or indirect word used in place of one that seems harsh or unpleasant

examples.text: "Relocation" was the regime's euphemism for forced exile.
The undertaker speaks only in euphemisms: "the departed," "at rest."
"Pre-owned" is a euphemism for "used."

confused.note: A euphemism is a mild substitute word; euphoria is intense happiness.

questions.passage: The company's long public announcement never once used the word "fired." It preferred a ______, stating that two hundred employees would be "released to pursue other opportunities."
questions.explanation: A mild phrase replacing a harsh word is a euphemism.

distractors.why: A panacea is a cure for everything, which does not fit.
A quagmire is a difficult situation, not a phrase.
A veneer is a false surface; the sentence concerns a choice of words, which is a euphemism.

definition: to invent something false in order to deceive; or to make or build

examples.text: The spy fabricated letters that seemed to prove the minister's treason.
The parts are fabricated from titanium in a single factory.
My brother fabricated an elaborate story to explain the broken window.

confused.note: To fabricate is to make or to make up; fabric is cloth.

questions.passage: The journalist was dismissed when editors discovered that he had ______ sources. Several of the experts quoted in his articles did not exist, and others said they had never spoken to him.
questions.explanation: Quoting people who do not exist is inventing them to deceive.

distractors.why: Exemplified means served as an example of, which does not fit.
Superseded means replaced, which does not fit.
Belittled means made to seem unimportant, which is not what he did to sources.

definition: not allowing something to pass through; not affected by something

examples.text: Clay is nearly impervious to water, which is why ponds are lined with it.
The fortress walls proved impervious to cannon fire.
My cat is impervious to scolding and goes right back on the counter.

confused.note: Impervious means unaffected or impenetrable; imperious means arrogantly commanding.

questions.passage: The veteran negotiator seemed ______ to pressure. Threats, flattery, and midnight deadlines all failed to move her, and she signed nothing until every clause was exactly as she wanted it.
questions.explanation: Being unmoved by every tactic shows she is unaffected.

distractors.why: Susceptible means easily affected, the opposite of this negotiator.
Erudite means learned, which does not complete "to pressure."
Elated means overjoyed, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin via, "way": no way through

definition: to make someone or something seem less important or impressive

examples.text: Rival newspapers belittled the explorer's achievement as mere luck.
The older brother belittles every poem the younger one writes.
Do not belittle your own progress just because someone else is faster.

confused.note: To belittle is to make something seem small; to bewilder is to confuse.

questions.passage: The coach never ______ her players' efforts. Even after a heavy defeat, she would find something each had done well and mention it before the whole team.
questions.explanation: Finding something to praise is the opposite of making their efforts seem small.

distractors.why: Exemplified means illustrated by example, which does not fit.
Fabricated means invented falsely, which does not fit.
Insinuated means hinted at something unpleasant, which does not fit "her players' efforts."

definition: matching something in size, amount, or importance

examples.text: The reward was commensurate with the danger of the voyage.
Funding should be commensurate with the scale of the problem.
My allowance is not commensurate with the number of chores I do.

confused.note: Commensurate means in proportion; commemorate means to honor the memory of.

questions.passage: The engineers argued that their salaries were not ______ with their responsibilities. Each was in charge of equipment worth millions, yet they earned less than the clerks who ordered the office supplies.
questions.explanation: Pay that does not match responsibility is out of proportion.

distractors.why: Impervious means unaffected, and "impervious with" is not idiomatic.
Preeminent means outstanding, which does not fit "with their responsibilities."
Tacit means unspoken, which does not fit.

definition: better or more important than all others

examples.text: For a century, the city was the preeminent port of the eastern sea.
She is the preeminent authority on deep-sea corals.
My grandmother is the preeminent pie baker of the entire county fair.

confused.note: Preeminent means the very best; prominent means well known or noticeable.

questions.passage: Among scholars of ancient languages, Dr. Farouk is ______. Her grammar is the standard text in every university, and no major translation is published without her review.
questions.explanation: Writing the standard text and reviewing every translation make her the leading scholar.

distractors.why: Nondescript means unremarkable, the opposite of the field's leading figure.
Sanctimonious means smugly moral, which is not what the evidence shows.
Voracious means having a huge appetite, which does not fit.

definition: something that people believe will solve all problems

examples.text: Reformers hailed the railway as a panacea for the nation's poverty.
Antibiotics are powerful, but they are not a panacea.
A nap is my panacea for nearly every bad mood.

confused.note: A panacea is a cure for everything; a placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient.

questions.passage: The new software will help teachers track attendance, but it is no ______. It cannot reduce class sizes, repair leaking roofs, or do anything about the shortage of textbooks.
questions.explanation: Software that cannot fix the other problems is not a cure for everything.

distractors.why: A quagmire is a hard situation to escape, which does not fit.
A euphemism is a mild substitute word, which does not fit.
An arbiter is a judge, which does not fit.

definition: wanting or eating great quantities of food; extremely eager for something

examples.text: The caterpillars are voracious and can strip a tree of leaves in a week.
A voracious reader, the heroine finishes the village library by twelve.
After swim practice I have a voracious appetite.

confused.note: Voracious means very hungry or eager; veracious means truthful.

questions.passage: Locusts are ______ feeders. A swarm covering a single square kilometer can eat as much in a day as thirty-five thousand people, leaving fields bare within hours of landing.
questions.explanation: Eating as much as thousands of people shows an enormous appetite.

distractors.why: Nondescript means unremarkable, which does not describe how much they eat.
Impervious means unaffected, which does not fit.
Erudite means learned, which does not describe insects.

definition: having or showing great knowledge gained from study

examples.text: The erudite monk could read nine languages.
The novel's erudite footnotes are longer than its chapters.
My erudite uncle answers every trivia question before the host finishes asking.

confused.note: Erudite is the adjective; erudition is the noun for deep learning.

questions.passage: The lecture was as ______ as its audience had expected. In ninety minutes the professor quoted from memory in four languages and traced a single proverb through two thousand years of literature.
questions.explanation: Quoting in four languages and tracing a proverb through centuries shows deep learning.

distractors.why: Nondescript means unremarkable, which this lecture was not.
Vindictive means vengeful, which does not fit.
Grandiose suggests empty showiness, but the lecture displayed real learning.

partsNote: from Latin rudis, "rough": brought out of roughness

definition: a difficult or complicated situation that is hard to escape; soft, wet ground

examples.text: The war became a quagmire that swallowed armies and treasure for a decade.
The field turned into a quagmire after a week of rain.
The group project became a quagmire of missed deadlines and blame.

confused.note: A quagmire is a sticky situation that traps you; a quandary is uncertainty about what to do.

questions.passage: What the firm had expected to be a simple lawsuit turned into a legal ______. Five years and three appeals later, the case had spread to courts in four countries, and neither side could find a way to end it.
questions.explanation: A case that keeps spreading with no way out is a situation hard to escape.

distractors.why: A panacea is a cure for all problems, the opposite of an endless tangle.
Clemency is mercy, which does not fit.
A euphemism is a mild expression, which does not fit.

definition: to be a typical example of something; to show by example

examples.text: The finch's beak exemplifies how a species adapts to its food supply.
The cathedral exemplifies the building style of its century.
My sister's color-coded binder exemplifies her love of order.

confused.note: Exemplify is the verb meaning to be an example of; exemplary is the adjective meaning model.

questions.passage: The town's main street ______ a trend seen across the region. Where a butcher, a baker, and a hardware store once stood, there are now three cafés, two phone shops, and a row of empty windows.
questions.explanation: The street is a typical example of the wider trend.

distractors.why: Supersedes means replaces, which does not fit a street and a trend.
Confounds means defies or confuses, but the street fits the trend.
Belittles means makes seem unimportant, which does not fit.

definition: to follow a winding course; to wander without a clear direction

examples.text: The river meanders across the plain in wide loops.
The story meanders through three generations before it finds its plot.
We meandered through the market with no plan and came home with a cactus.

confused.note: To meander is to wander along a winding course; to maunder is to talk in a rambling way.

questions.passage: The path does not climb directly to the summit. It ______ through the forest, doubling back on itself a dozen times, so that a peak only two kilometers away takes most of a morning to reach.
questions.explanation: A path that doubles back many times follows a winding course.

distractors.why: Supersedes means replaces, which does not fit.
Insinuates means hints slyly, which does not describe a path.
Fabricates means invents or builds, which does not fit.

definition: to take the place of something older or less effective

examples.text: The printed book superseded the handwritten manuscript within a century.
The new measurement supersedes the estimate published in 2010.
The group chat has superseded the family phone tree.

confused.note: To supersede is to replace; to surpass is to do better than.

questions.passage: The 1998 guidelines are no longer in force. They were ______ last year by a new set of rules that doubles the required inspections and applies to smaller factories as well.
questions.explanation: New rules replaced the old guidelines.

distractors.why: Exemplified means illustrated, which does not fit.
Belittled means made to seem unimportant; the guidelines were replaced, not mocked.
Fabricated means invented falsely, which does not fit.

definition: to confuse and surprise someone; to prove a prediction or expectation wrong

examples.text: The results confounded researchers, who had predicted the opposite.
The small republic confounded its enemies by surviving the winter.
My grandmother confounded us all by winning the video game tournament.

confused.note: To confound is to confuse or defy expectation; to compound is to make worse or to combine.

questions.passage: Experts had predicted that the newspaper would close within a year. It ______ them: a decade later it is still printing, and its circulation has grown in each of the last five years.
questions.explanation: The paper's survival proved the experts' prediction wrong and surprised them.

distractors.why: Exemplified would mean it was a typical case of what they predicted, the opposite of what happened.
Insinuated means hinted slyly, which does not fit.
Meandered means wandered, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin fundere, "to pour": to pour together, to mix up

definition: having no interesting or unusual features; ordinary

examples.text: The spy lives in a nondescript house on a nondescript street.
The treaty was signed in a nondescript office above a bakery.
I drive a nondescript gray car that I can never find in a parking lot.

confused.note: Nondescript means ordinary and featureless; nonchalant means casually calm.

questions.passage: Nothing about the building hints at what it contains. From the street it is a ______ brick warehouse like a dozen others on the block, yet behind its unmarked door is one of the finest collections of rare maps in the world.
questions.explanation: A warehouse like a dozen others has no distinctive features.

distractors.why: Grandiose means showy and overambitious, the opposite of a plain warehouse.
Preeminent means outstanding, which describes the collection, not the building's appearance.
Impervious means impenetrable or unaffected, which is not the point.

definition: to suggest something unpleasant in an indirect way

examples.text: The cousin insinuates that the will was changed under pressure.
Pamphlets insinuated that the queen's ministers were in foreign pay.
Are you insinuating that I ate the last slice?

confused.note: To insinuate is to hint at something unpleasant; to instigate is to start trouble.

questions.passage: The article never accused the mayor of taking bribes. It merely ______ as much, noting that he had bought a second home shortly after awarding the contract and asking "where the money came from."
questions.explanation: Raising pointed questions without a direct accusation is hinting.

distractors.why: Fabricated means invented falsely, which is not what "merely" hinting describes.
Confounded means baffled, which does not fit.
Superseded means replaced, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin sinus, "curve": to wind one's way in

definition: acting as if you are morally better than other people

examples.text: The sanctimonious deacon lectures the village on thrift while hiding his debts.
Readers tired of the editor's sanctimonious attacks on other people's vices.
My brother gets sanctimonious about recycling whenever I forget.

confused.note: Sanctimonious means smugly moral; a sanctuary is a safe or holy place.

questions.passage: Colleagues found the director's speeches ______. He reminded them weekly of his own honesty and hard work and suggested, with a sorrowful shake of the head, that others might learn from his example.
questions.explanation: Praising his own virtue and lecturing others shows he acts morally superior.

distractors.why: Erudite means learned, which is not what annoyed his colleagues.
Nondescript means unremarkable, which does not describe boastful speeches.
Commensurate means proportionate, which does not fit.

definition: dishonest behavior meant to trick someone; double-dealing

examples.text: The ambassador's duplicity was exposed when both kings compared his letters.
The heroine never suspects the duplicity of her smiling guardian.
I discovered my brother's duplicity when I found my "lost" charger in his room.

confused.note: Duplicity is deceit; duplication is copying.

questions.passage: The agent's ______ was discovered only by accident. For six years he had sold the same secrets to two rival governments, assuring each that it was his only employer.
questions.explanation: Selling to both sides while lying to each is double-dealing.

distractors.why: Clemency is mercy, which does not fit.
Integrity is honesty, the opposite of his conduct.
A euphemism is a mild expression, which does not fit.
